newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan backs Cuba asylum for Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Japan backs Cuba asylum for Peru rebels.

text.p: Japan on Tuesday threw its weight behind a proposal to resolve the Lima hostage crisis by allowing Marxist rebels to go to Cuba and called for international support for the plan.

The plea follows a meeting between Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and Cuban leader Fidel Castro on Monday in Havana, after which Castro said he was willing to accept some 20 Marxist rebels who have held 72 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for more than two months.

It was the first time since the rebels stormed the residence during a cocktail party on December 17 to grab the hostages that a third country has said it is willing to accept the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas in exchange for freeing the hostages.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday told reporters he had instructed Terusuke Terada, the top Japanese diplomat in Lima, to meet Fujimori as soon as he returned from Havana.
"After hearing (Terada's) report, we must work towards creating an international atmosphere and international opinion (favourable to the plan)," Hashimoto said.
Hashimoto did not elaborate, but government sources said his remarks indicated he would seek support from the United States, an avowed enemy of Cuba, for the proposal.
From the start, Cuba has been cited in media reports as a possible mediator in the crisis, or as a place of refuge for the rebels.
"It's a moral duty (to accept the guerrillas)," Castro told reporters after seeing Fujimori off at Havana airport.
Top Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama welcomed Fujimori's plan by saying it would be an effective way to resolve the crisis peacefully.

"I will not say whether this is morally right or wrong," Kajiyama told a regular news conference. "I think it is an effective way both in terms of not giving in to terrorism and of ending this peacefully."
Kajiyama said he understood that both the Japanese and Peruvian governments must make formal requests to Cuba if such an exchange was to be carried out.
Japanese government sources said the outcome was still unclear in the 76-day-old crisis.
"Of course we are aware of the difficulties even if the Cuban plan goes ahead," one government official said.
The question remained whether the rebels holding the hostages would agree to a deal involving them taking asylum abroad.
In Pamplona, Spain, a spokesman for the MRTA in Europe said the MRTA rebels would not accept exile.
"We are not thinking about leaving Peru," spokesman Isaac Velasco told reporters before news of Cuba's position emerged.
The heavily armed Tupac Amaru guerrillas captured hundreds of hostages when they stormed the residence, but released most of them to keep 72 heavyweight bargaining chips.
Their main demand is the release of 400 comrades from Peruvian jails. Fujimori has ruled this out, but has hinted at other concessions.
